F.1 Subspace Initialization
Figure 14: For all low-rank MLPs with 𝑼~\widetilde{\bm{U}} and 𝑽~\widetilde{\bm{V}} initialized close to (ψ≤45\psi\leq 45 degrees) 𝑼~b​i​g\widetilde{\bm{U}}_{big} and 𝑽~b​i​g\widetilde{\bm{V}}_{big}, GD reaches similar solutions. Otherwise, GD gets stuck in progressively worse local minima as ψ\psi increases.
[id=A6.SS1.p1.1] From Figures 6 and 7 in Sections 5.1.1 and 5.1.2 respectively, we observe that if we train the low-rank MLP in (10) after initializing 𝑼~\widetilde{\bm{U}} and 𝑽~\widetilde{\bm{V}} as random semi-orthogonal matrices (green), then (S)GD gets stuck in a much worse local minimum compared to the other MLPs (blue and orange). In this section, we ablate the initialization of 𝑼~\widetilde{\bm{U}} and 𝑽~\widetilde{\bm{V}}.
[id=A6.SS1.SSS0.Px1]
Experimental details.
[id=A6.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p1.1] We repeated the experiments as described in Section 5.1.1. We used the exact same training algorithm (full batch GD), hyperparameters, and loss function (total squared-error loss). However, we only used ϕ=SiLU\phi=\operatorname{SiLU}, and we varied the initialization of 𝑼~\widetilde{\bm{U}} and 𝑽~\widetilde{\bm{V}} as follows. First, we define 𝑼~b​i​g∈ℝd×r\widetilde{\bm{U}}_{big}\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times r} and 𝑽~b​i​g∈ℝd×r\widetilde{\bm{V}}_{big}\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times r} to be the result of the 𝒮b​i​g\mathcal{S}_{big} initialization scheme described in Section 5, where we set r=2​K=20r=2K=20. Next, we define 𝑼~b​i​g⟂,𝑽~b​i​g⟂∈ℝd×r\widetilde{\bm{U}}_{big}^{\perp},\widetilde{\bm{V}}_{big}^{\perp}\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times r} to be completely orthogonal to 𝑼~b​i​g\widetilde{\bm{U}}_{big} and 𝑽~b​i​g\widetilde{\bm{V}}_{big}, respectively. Finally, we initialized 𝑼~\widetilde{\bm{U}} and 𝑽~\widetilde{\bm{V}} to be some angle ψ\psi degrees away from 𝑼~b​i​g\widetilde{\bm{U}}_{big} and 𝑽~b​i​g\widetilde{\bm{V}}_{big} via
[id=A6.EGx123]
𝑼~=cos⁡(ψ)⋅𝑼~b​i​g+sin⁡(ψ)⋅𝑼~b​i​g⟂and𝑽~=cos⁡(ψ)⋅𝑽~b​i​g+sin⁡(ψ)⋅𝑽~b​i​g⟂.\displaystyle\widetilde{\bm{U}}=\cos\left(\psi\right)\cdot\widetilde{\bm{U}}_{big}+\sin\left(\psi\right)\cdot\widetilde{\bm{U}}_{big}^{\perp}\quad\text{and}\quad\widetilde{\bm{V}}=\cos(\psi)\cdot\widetilde{\bm{V}}_{big}+\sin(\psi)\cdot\widetilde{\bm{V}}_{big}^{\perp}.
(18)
[id=A6.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p1.2] In our experiments, we swept through ψ∈{0,15,30,45,60,75,90}\psi\in\{0,15,30,45,60,75,90\} degrees.
[id=A6.SS1.SSS0.Px2]
Results.
[id=A6.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p1.1] Figure 14 shows the resulting test loss and accuracy curves during training averaged over 55 trials for each ψ\psi. The test loss and accuracy curves are nearly identical for all ψ∈{0,15,30,45}\psi\in\{0,15,30,45\} degrees, although at ψ=45\psi=45, GD required slightly more iterations for the test loss to begin decreasing from its initial value. The performance noticeably deteriorates when ψ>45\psi>45. For ψ∈{60,75}\psi\in\{60,75\} degrees, the test loss still decreases from their initial values, but GD gets stuck in noticeably worse local minima compared to when ψ<45\psi<45. Finally, at ψ=90\psi=90, the initialized 𝑼~\widetilde{\bm{U}} and 𝑽~\widetilde{\bm{V}} are completely orthogonal to 𝑼~b​i​g\widetilde{\bm{U}}_{big} and 𝑽~b​i​g\widetilde{\bm{V}}_{big}. The test loss stays at its initial value for all training epochs, and the low-rank MLP does not escape the random guessing stage. Overall, if 𝑼~\widetilde{\bm{U}} / 𝑽~\widetilde{\bm{V}} in the low-rank MLP are initialized to be closer to 𝑼~b​i​g\widetilde{\bm{U}}_{big} / 𝑽~b​i​g\widetilde{\bm{V}}_{big} than their orthogonal complements, then the low-rank MLP can eventually nearly match the performance of the full-rank counterpart. Otherwise, GD gets stuck in progressively worse local minima as ψ→90\psi\to 90 degrees.
[id=A6.SS2]
F.2 Width Ablation
Figure 15: Increasing the width rr of the low-rank MLP initially leads to a noticeable increase in test accuracy, but further increasing rr leads to diminishing returns in test accuracy gains. Here, we only trained the classifier head in VGG-16, and kept the convolutional layers frozen at their ImageNet pre-trained weights.
[id=A6.SS2.p1.1] From the classifier-only results in Section 5.1.2 (Figure 7), there is a 5−10%5-10\% gap in test accuracy between the low-rank MLP with 𝒮b​i​g\mathcal{S}_{big} initialization (orange) and the fully parameterized MLP (blue). In this section, we investigate how much does this gap close by increasing the width rr.
[id=A6.SS2.SSS0.Px1]
Experimental details.
[id=A6.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1.1] We repeated the classifier-only training experiments as described in Section 5.1.2 with both ϕ=GELU\phi=\operatorname{GELU} and ϕ=SiLU\phi=\operatorname{SiLU}, again using the exact same training algorithm (SGD with momentum), hyperparameters, and loss function (cross-entropy loss). However, now we vary the width r∈{2​K,4​K,8​K,16​K}r\in\{2K,4K,8K,16K\} in the low-rank MLP in (10). We initialized 𝑼~\widetilde{\bm{U}} and 𝑽~\widetilde{\bm{V}} using the 𝒮b​i​g\mathcal{S}_{big} initialization scheme as described in Section 5. For r>2​Kr>2K, we initialized the last r−2​Kr-2K columns of 𝑼~\widetilde{\bm{U}} and 𝑽~\widetilde{\bm{V}} to lie in the orthogonal complements of their first 2​K2K columns.
[id=A6.SS2.SSS0.Px2]
Results.
[id=A6.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1.1] Figure 15 shows the test accuracy at every training epoch for each rr. Even going from r=2​Kr=2K to r=4​Kr=4K noticeably closes the gap between the low-rank and fully-parameterized MLPs, especially for the SiLU\operatorname{SiLU} classifier. However, continuing to double rr further leads to diminishing returns in performance gains. Nevertheless, with the appropriate initialization on 𝑼~\widetilde{\bm{U}} and 𝑽~\widetilde{\bm{V}}, a width of r=Θ⁡(K)r=\Theta(K) appears to be sufficient in achieving a test accuracy that is only about 2−3%2-3\% lower than that of the fully parameterized classifier head.
